t: Find Minimum Time to Finish All Jobs — Pruned Search and Subset DP
o:
We must hand every job to exactly one of k workers so that the busiest worker’s total load is minimized. Example 1 (jobs = [3,2,3], k = 3) is trivial: one job each, answer 3. Example 2 (jobs = [1,2,4,7,8], k = 2) shows why balancing matters: grouping {1,2,8} and {4,7} leaves both workers at 11, and no split does better.
The constraints are the loudest hint in the problem: n ≤ 12 and k ≤ 12. That invites exponential-in-n algorithms — pruned exhaustive assignment or subset dynamic programming — since this is essentially multiway number partitioning, for which no polynomial algorithm is expected. Two very different tools fit the budget: backtracking with strong symmetry pruning (fast in practice) and a bitmask DP whose cost is provably O(k · 3^n) thanks to submask enumeration.
k: n ≤ 12 makes exponential subset algorithms affordable; the problem is number partitioning, so polynomial tricks are not expected.
Sorting jobs descending and skipping workers with equal current loads prunes the assignment tree dramatically.
Submask iteration ((sub − 1) & mask) enumerates all subsets of every mask in 3^n steps total, not 4^n.
Extra workers beyond n never help, so DP layers can be capped at min(k, n).

a.i: Process jobs one at a time, trying each worker for each job, and track the best (smallest) maximum load found. Raw search is k^n branches, but three prunings tame it: sort jobs descending so large jobs are placed while the tree is shallow; abandon a branch the moment its current maximum reaches the best answer so far; and skip a worker whose load equals one already tried at this level — assigning the next job to either is symmetric and cannot produce new outcomes.
s: Sort jobs in descending order; initialize all worker loads to zero and best = sum(jobs).
DFS on job index i with running maximum cur; stop the branch if cur ≥ best.
For each worker not duplicating an already-tried load value at this level, add jobs[i] and recurse.
When all jobs are placed, update best with cur; return best at the end.
a.t: O(k^n) worst case, heavily pruned by sorting, symmetry-skipping, and best-so-far cutoffs; comfortably fast for n ≤ 12.
a.sp: O(n + k) — recursion depth plus the loads array.

a.n: Approach 2: Bitmask DP over Job Subsets
a.i: Number jobs 0..n−1 and treat any partial assignment as a subset mask of covered jobs. Precompute sums[mask] once using the lowest set bit trick. Let dp[mask] be the least possible maximum working time when the jobs in mask are shared among j workers; worker j takes some nonempty submask sub in one gulp, giving dp_new[mask] = min over sub ⊆ mask of max(dp[mask XOR sub], sums[sub]). Iterating every submask of every mask costs 3^n per layer (about 5·10^5 for n = 12), times k layers.
s: Precompute sums[mask] for all 2^n masks via sums[mask] = sums[mask without lowest bit] + jobs[lowest bit index].
Initialize dp = sums, the answer with one worker.
Repeat k − 1 times: recompute dp[mask] by enumerating every nonempty submask sub of mask and taking min(max(previous dp[mask XOR sub], sums[sub])).
a.t: O(k · 3^n) — each of the k layers enumerates the submasks of all masks (≈6.4 · 10^6 operations at n = k = 12).
a.sp: O(2^n) — two DP arrays of subset states.

w: Open with backtracking if you want quick, convincing code, then offer the bitmask DP as the solution with a hard runtime guarantee — interviewers specifically like hearing the 3^n submask-enumeration trick. Pitfalls: forgetting the descending sort (pruning quality collapses), allowing duplicate-load branches (symmetry explosion), and overflowing fixed-width integers in other settings (here 12 × 10^7 fits in int, but say so). Edge cases: k ≥ n means the answer is simply the largest job; a single job; all-equal jobs. Follow-ups: workers with different speed factors (weight each subset by the worker it lands on), jobs that may be split across workers, or counting the number of optimal assignments.
